content.title: About
content.content: Asparagus is the young shoot of the plant Asparagus officinalis, typically harvested in spring. Cooked asparagus retains a delicate flavor, crisp texture, and bright green color. It is rich in vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus is one of the oldest cultivated vegetables, with a history of over 2,000 years.
In ancient Rome, asparagus was served only to the emperor and the elite.
There are more than 300 varieties of asparagus, differing in spear thickness and taste.
Asparagus contains aromatic compounds that give it its distinctive smell.
The United States imports over 1 billion pounds of asparagus each year.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate supports cell division and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Glutathione, vitamin C, and vitamin E help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: About 2 g of protein per 100 g makes asparagus a good addition to calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to asparagus, manifested as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Asparagus contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage can cause spoilage, leading to possible food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked asparagus can be served as a side dish, added to salads, omelets, pasta, or soups. For extra flavor, drizzle with olive oil and sprinkle with lemon juice or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store asparagus in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container, lightly wrapped in a damp cloth, for up to 3‑4 days. To freeze, blanch for 2‑3 minutes, shock in ice water, then pack in an airtight bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Chinese broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. alboglabra), also known as gai lan or Chinese kale, is a leafy vegetable with thick stems and large, tender leaves. When cooked briefly, it has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a pleasant crunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: It belongs to the cruciferous family, the same as regular broccoli, cauliflower and cabbage.
In China it is a staple in stir‑fries, soups and as a side dish for rice.
Chinese broccoli contains higher levels of glucosinolates than its Western counterpart, boosting its antioxidant potential.
In Japan it is sometimes called “nori‑naru” and served cold after blanching.
A quick boil (1–3 minutes) preserves its vivid green color and most of its nutrients.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: A serving provides over 100 % of the daily value for vitamin C, supporting immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health, and Chinese broccoli is a very good source.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate (vitamin B9) is important for DNA synthesis and especially crucial during pregnancy.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Glucosinolates and carotenoids help neutralize free radicals and may reduce the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Large amounts of glucosinolates can interfere with thyroid function in susceptible individuals; moderation is advised.

items.title: Nutrient loss with overcooking
items.content: Prolonged boiling destroys heat‑sensitive vitamins, especially vitamin C and folate.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may be allergic to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chinese broccoli is typically blanched in boiling water for 1–3 minutes, then shocked in ice water to retain color and crunch. It can be added to salads, soups, stir‑fries, served as a side to rice or noodles, or tossed with garlic and sesame oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh heads in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container with a damp paper towel for 3–5 days. Cooked broccoli should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 2–3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Falafel is a deep‑fried ball made from ground chickpeas (sometimes mixed with fava beans), herbs and spices. It is a staple snack in the Middle East and Mediterranean, often served in pita bread or with tahini sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional falafel is made from dried chickpeas that are soaked, not from canned beans.
It is believed to have originated in Egypt, where it is called "ta’amiya".
In Israel falafel is considered a national street food and is sold by countless vendors.
Recipes vary widely – common additions include green onion, parsley, cilantro, cumin, and coriander.
Falafel can be baked for a healthier version, but classic preparation involves deep‑frying for a crisp crust.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Chickpeas provide about 20 % protein, making falafel a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are important for blood formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Falafel raises blood sugar slowly, which can help with glucose control.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Spices such as cumin and coriander add antioxidant compounds that combat free radicals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chickpeas.

items.title: High fat content when fried
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant oil, increasing the calorie density.

items.title: Salt and spice excess
items.content: Too much salt can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Contamination risk if stored improperly
items.content: Dry chickpeas can develop mycotoxins when kept in humid conditions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot falafel in pita with lettuce, tomatoes, cucumber, and tahini sauce, or enjoy it with hummus. It also works well added to salads, soups, or as a snack on its own.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry chickpeas in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked falafel should be refrigerated and consumed within 2‑3 days, or frozen for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat lasagna is a classic Italian dish made of layers of pasta sheets, meat sauce (usually ground beef), tomato sauce, cheese and sometimes béchamel. It is baked until the top turns golden, resulting in a flavorful and hearty dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first written mention of lasagna dates back to the 13th century, but the modern meat‑based version became popular in the United States in the early 20th century.
The word “lasagna” comes from the Latin “lasanum,” meaning “cooking pot.”
In the United States, July 29 is celebrated as National Lasagna Day.
Traditional Italian lasagna often uses a ragù (meat ragout) rather than plain ground beef.
There are more than 30 recognized variations of lasagna, including vegetarian, seafood and even dessert versions.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat in the dish provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Hard cheeses add calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant linked to heart health.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of carbs, fats and protein makes lasagna a substantial source of energy for active individuals.

items.title: High calorie and fat content
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for those monitoring weight.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cheese and prepared sauces often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with dairy sensitivities should choose lactose‑free or dairy‑free cheese alternatives.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked ground meat may harbor pathogens; ensure the meat reaches an internal temperature of 71 °C (160 °F).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lasagna is typically cut into serving portions and served hot, sprinkled with fresh basil or grated Parmesan. It pairs well with a light salad, garlic bread, and a glass of red wine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, portion and freeze in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months. Reheat until the interior reaches 74 °C (165 °F).

content.title: About
content.content: Peppers, hot, cooked are thermally processed fruits of the hot Capsicum varieties, commonly used in cuisine to add heat and aroma. After cooking they retain a bright color, tender texture, and characteristic spicy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hot peppers contain capsaicin – the compound responsible for the burning sensation.
Capsaicin is used in medicine and cosmetics for its anti‑inflammatory and analgesic properties.
Cooked hot peppers are often added to sauces, soups, and marinades.
Vitamin C content in hot peppers exceeds that of many citrus fruits.
Peppers come in various colors – red, yellow, orange – each with different levels of sweetness and heat.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains capsaicin
items.content: Capsaicin may boost metabolism and has a thermogenic effect.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and flavonoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Capsaicin helps dilate blood vessels and improve circulation.

items.title: Contains vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A is essential for vision and skin health.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: People with sensitive stomachs may experience discomfort or heartburn from very spicy foods.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to capsaicin.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Capsaicin can enhance the effects of certain anticoagulants.

items.title: Skin burns
items.content: When handling fresh hot peppers, avoid skin and eye contact to prevent irritation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked hot peppers can be added to soups, stews, sauces, salads, and pizza. They are also used as fillings for sandwiches or as a side dish for meat. If desired, blend them into a paste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked peppers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags – they will keep flavor and aroma for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Lean pork chop is a cut taken from the loin or rib area of the pig after the excess fat has been trimmed away. It is known for its mild flavor, low fat content, and high protein level. The chop is commonly grilled, baked, or pan‑seared.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lean chops are usually sourced from the tenderloin or loin where fat is less than 5 %.
Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide, especially in Europe and Asia.
When cooked properly, lean pork remains juicy and tender despite its low fat content.
Traditional cuisines often marinate chops in herbs, spices, and acidic ingredients (lemon, vinegar) to enhance flavor.
Pork is a good source of vitamin B12, essential for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Lean pork chops provide about 20‑22 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: With most visible fat removed, these chops fit well into calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3 and B6 aid metabolism and help maintain energy levels.

items.title: Minerals: zinc and selenium
items.content: Zinc supports immune function, while selenium provides antioxidant protection.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Pork contains phosphorus, which works with calcium to maintain strong bones.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor pathogens (Salmonella, Trichinella). Cook to an internal temperature of 63 °C.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork.

items.title: Sodium in processed versions
items.content: Pre‑marinated or cured chops can be high in salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People with gout should monitor intake, as pork contains moderate levels of purines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chops can be pan‑seared, baked, grilled, or braised in a sauce. Lightly pounding the meat helps it cook evenly. Serve with vegetables, whole grains, or a light sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh chops in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 4 months. Thaw frozen chops in the fridge before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Raccoon is an innovative product designed to address home automation challenges. It combines compact design, high performance, and easy integration with other smart devices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “Raccoon” reflects the product’s ability to adapt to various environments, just like the animal in nature.
The product supports over 20 communication protocols, including Wi‑Fi, Zigbee, and Bluetooth Low Energy.
Raccoon is ENERGY STAR certified, demonstrating energy efficiency.
Inside the device is a quad‑core processor that ensures fast data processing.
Developers added a self‑learning feature that lets the system optimize its operation based on user behavior.

items.title: Smart Control
items.content: Enables management of lighting, climate, and security through a single interface.

items.title: Energy Efficiency
items.content: Reduces electricity consumption by intelligently scheduling device operation.

items.title: Flexible Integration
items.content: Easily connects with existing smart‑home systems from various manufacturers.

items.title: Data Security
items.content: AES‑256 level encryption protects personal information and settings.

items.title: Over‑the‑Air Updates
items.content: Automatically receives new features and bug fixes without user intervention.

items.title: Compatibility
items.content: Some older devices may not support newer protocols and might require an additional adapter.

items.title: Network Requirements
items.content: A stable 2.4 GHz Wi‑Fi network is recommended for reliable operation.

items.title: Privacy
items.content: Users should regularly review access settings to avoid unintended data sharing.

items.title: Firmware Updates
items.content: During updates the device may need to be temporarily disconnected.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Connect Raccoon to your Wi‑Fi network, download the app, follow the setup wizard, and add your devices. Once synced, you can control all functions via smartphone, voice assistants, or a web interface.

content.title: Storage and Maintenance
content.content: Store the device in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. If needed, clean the exterior with a dry soft cloth. Regularly check for firmware updates through the app.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned meat‑filled ravioli in tomato sauce is a ready‑to‑eat product made from wheat flour pasta, a blend of beef and pork mince, and a seasoned tomato sauce. It is packed in hermetically sealed glass or metal cans, providing a long shelf life without refrigeration.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ravioli originate from Italy and have been prepared for over a thousand years.
Traditional meat filling combines beef and pork, but regional variations exist.
The tomato sauce is often enriched with basil, oregano, and garlic for extra aroma.
Canning preserves nutrients and flavor for 12–24 months.
Canned ravioli became popular in Russia in the 1990s as a convenient quick‑meal option.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The meat filling provides about 10 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes and meat deliver vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Thermally processed ravioli are suitable for people with sensitive digestion because they are fully cooked.

items.title: Convenient calorie source
items.content: The balance of fats and carbohydrates makes the product a quick energy source, useful when time is limited.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains significant salt; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat‑based dough can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Preservatives may be added for shelf stability, which some consumers prefer to avoid.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A typical can (≈250 g) provides about 300–350 kcal, which may be excessive for calorie‑restricted diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat after opening the can. Heat it in the microwave (2–3 minutes) or on the stovetop, then garnish with fresh herbs, grated cheese, or a drizzle of olive oil. Serve with a green salad or crusty bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, refrigerate and consume within 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp salad is a dish made with boiled or sautéed shrimp, fresh vegetables such as cucumber, tomato, and lettuce, often complemented by avocado, hard‑boiled eggs, and a light dressing based on olive oil, lemon juice or yogurt. The shrimp give the salad a delicate sea flavor and a high protein content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp belong to the crustacean family and are among the most consumed seafood worldwide.
There are more than 2,000 shrimp species, but culinary dishes most often use tiger, royal, and northern varieties.
Shrimp can change the color of their shells in response to stress and environment.
In Japan, shrimp salads are popular and often served with soy sauce and wasabi.
Shrimp are rich in astaxanthin, a powerful antioxidant that gives them their pink hue.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Only about 99 kcal per 100 g, making the salad a light option for weight control.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s promote heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B12 and B6 are important for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Shrimp are a good source of selenium, zinc, and iron, which support immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Microbial contamination risk
items.content: Improperly handled or stored shrimp can harbor salmonella or vibrio bacteria.

items.title: High sodium in ready‑made dressings
items.content: Pre‑made sauces often contain a lot of salt; it’s better to prepare the dressing yourself.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve shrimp salad chilled or slightly cooled. Toss shrimp with mixed greens, sliced vegetables, avocado, and hard‑boiled eggs; dress with olive oil and lemon juice, balsamic vinegar, or a light yogurt sauce. Garnish with fresh herbs or seeds if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days at most. Store cooked shrimp at 0‑4 °C and use within a day of cooking. Discard if you notice an off‑odor or discoloration.
